profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal troubleshooting meeting is being held by a Kaiser Permanente Mid-Atlantic research team after a refreshed claims-plus-EHR extract produced lower-than-expected rates of antecedent ED treat-and-release diagnoses before sepsis hospitalization, weakening the previously observed FED and AMS signals in a SPADE analysis. The immediate context is that the team must reconcile why the rerun no longer matches counts used in a draft methods memo before presenting to an internal epidemiology review group. The agenda is to compare cohort construction decisions, inspect how antecedent ED visits are being linked to the sepsis hospitalization, and determine which implementation detail is driving the discrepancy. The expected outcome is a concrete troubleshooting plan for reruns and audit tables, not a final scientific conclusion.

members.name: Dr. Nina Patel
members.role: Emergency physician investigator and clinical lead
members.expertise: Sepsis recognition, diagnostic error in emergency care, ED discharge decision-making, clinical interpretation of administrative data
members.background: Board-certified emergency physician at an integrated delivery system who has led chart-review studies on missed infections and now serves as the clinical PI for the sepsis SPADE project.
members.private_state: She wants the analysis to preserve clinical face validity before internal review and is especially worried that operational coding choices are stripping out the exact bounce-back cases that feel like delayed diagnosis to frontline physicians.
hidden_assumptions: The 'hospitalization date' for a sepsis episode starts when the patient first presents for the acute return visit, even if administrative inpatient status is assigned later.
A patient who leaves the ED without being admitted to an inpatient bed that day counts as 'treat-and-release,' including short observation pathways that end at home.
FED and AMS should reflect the clinician's working impression at discharge, so related diagnoses documented anywhere on the ED discharge record are part of the signal, not just the principal code.
When a symptom cluster appears just before admission, the goal of SPADE is to capture clinically plausible missed opportunities rather than only perfectly clean claims-defined episodes.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Claims adjudication structure, EHR-claims linkage, ICD-9/10 crosswalks, reproducible SPADE pipeline implementation
members.background: Master's-trained health services analyst who maintains the system's longitudinal utilization datasets and previously built a reusable pipeline for identifying antecedent visits before index hospitalizations.
members.private_state: He wants a defensible, reproducible specification that can be rerun without hand-tuning and is concerned that clinically intuitive exceptions will make counts unstable across data refreshes and coding eras.
hidden_assumptions: The 'index hospitalization date' should be anchored to the first inpatient claim or service date because that is the most stable event across data sources.
An ED encounter is only 'treat-and-release' if the administrative disposition is home and there are no attached observation or inpatient revenue codes for that episode.
Clinical categories such as FED or AMS should be populated from the pre-specified primary ED diagnosis code lists used in the prior analytic script for comparability.
If the earlier pipeline was already circulated internally, downstream terminology like 'same logic as before' refers to that codified implementation rather than a broader clinical intent.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the index hospitalization date
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the 'hospitalization date' or the 'month before hospitalization' as though it is a single obvious anchor.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the patient's acute return presentation date for the sepsis episode, including the ED arrival that later converts to admission.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the first inpatient claim/service date recorded for the sepsis stay, which can be later than the ED arrival date.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In hospital research work, 'hospitalization date' sounds standard and settled, and both anchors usually coincide closely enough that neither expects the phrase itself to need unpacking.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they are counting 'treat-and-release ED visits' and assume they are discussing the same pool of antecedent encounters.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes ED visits that route through short observation and still end with the patient going home, because clinically the patient was evaluated and released rather than admitted.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 excludes any encounter with observation billing or an attached overnight episode, because administratively it is no longer a clean ED discharge-home event.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Observation status occupies a gray zone between clinical workflow and billing logic, so each person treats their interpretation as the obvious meaning of an otherwise familiar phrase.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the 'FED signal' and 'AMS signal' as if the category definitions were already shared from the prior run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the signal should include clinically related dehydration, hyponatremia, delirium, confusion, and similar codes documented anywhere relevant on the ED discharge record because they represent the diagnostic impression being acted on.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the signal is generated by the existing codebook applied to the primary ED diagnosis field only, with no expansion to secondary fields or clinically adjacent codes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are invoking the same category labels from prior work, each believes the operational details are already embedded in the shared shorthand and not something that needs restating.

turns.inner_thought: The refreshed extract shouldn't have wiped out the exact bounce-back patterns the clinicians recognize. If the FED and AMS signals are collapsing, something operational changed in how antecedent visits are being counted, and I need to steer this back toward clinical face validity before epi review.
turns.utterance: I want to start with the big discrepancy. In the refreshed SPADE rerun, the sepsis denominator looked roughly where I expected, but the antecedent ED treat-and-release diagnoses before hospitalization dropped enough that the FED signal and AMS signal both weakened. Can we walk through where that count changed?

turns.inner_thought: The cohort itself is stable; the shift came from rebuilding the look-back in the reproducible pipeline. I anchored the month-before window to the first inpatient claim/service date from the inpatient file because that's the cleanest, most stable hospitalization date across refreshes and data sources.
turns.utterance: Yes. The sepsis cohort itself is pretty stable. What moved was the antecedent ED pool after I rebuilt the month-before window off the index hospitalization date from the inpatient file. Once I applied that consistently, fewer visits landed in the pre-hospitalization period.

turns.inner_thought: If the patient comes back to the ED and that acute return leads into the sepsis stay, that return presentation is the start of the hospitalization episode for our purposes, even if inpatient status posts later. Otherwise we shave off the clinically important near-miss window.
turns.utterance: That may explain some of it, but the month before hospitalization should still be catching those bounce-back ED discharges. From the clinical side, when the patient comes back acutely, that hospitalization episode has effectively started, so I wouldn't expect those cases to fall away.

turns.inner_thought: Another major drop came from applying my usual strict treat-and-release definition: home disposition only, no observation or inpatient revenue codes attached to the episode. A lot of the borderline cases disappeared once linked observation claims showed up in the refreshed data.
turns.utterance: There was a second change too. A fair number of borderline encounters stopped counting as treat-and-release ED visits once the refreshed linkage showed observation claims attached to the same episode. That narrowed the antecedent visit pool quite a bit.

turns.inner_thought: If they were watched briefly and still went home, those are exactly the patients frontline physicians would consider evaluated and released, not admitted. Excluding observation-home pathways strips out some of the most plausible delayed-diagnosis cases.
turns.utterance: Right, and that's where I get nervous. Patients who were watched briefly and then sent home are exactly the kind of treat-and-release cases I would expect the look-back to include. Clinically, those are still part of the signal we're trying to understand.

turns.inner_thought: I also kept the FED logic exactly as in the prior script for comparability: the pre-specified codebook on the primary ED diagnosis field only. If I start expanding to other fields or adjacent diagnoses ad hoc, the rerun won't be cleanly comparable to the earlier circulated implementation.
turns.utterance: And separately, the FED signal weakened because I kept the prior category logic the same as before. I used the existing FED mapping on the primary ED diagnosis field so the rerun would stay aligned with the current script.

turns.inner_thought: When I say FED and AMS, I'm thinking about the ED clinician's working impression at discharge, not just whichever code landed first. Dehydration, hyponatremia, confusion, delirium—those are part of the same clinical picture and should be counted if they're on the discharge record.
turns.utterance: I think we may be using those labels a little more narrowly than I am. When I talk about the FED signal and AMS signal, I'm thinking about the ED working diagnosis pattern at discharge, including the related dehydration, sodium abnormality, confusion, and delirium documentation that shows up there.

turns.inner_thought: This is also why the temporal spike flattened. Once I anchored same-episode returns to the inpatient service date rather than the ED arrival that rolled into admission, the clustering right near hospitalization was less pronounced. That felt methodologically cleaner to me.
turns.utterance: One thing I noticed in the plots is that the clustering right near admission flattened out once same-episode returns were anchored to the hospitalization date coming from the inpatient side rather than the earlier ED touchpoint tied to that stay.

turns.inner_thought: We need a case-based audit, not just aggregate counts. I want to see next-day admissions, observation-home discharges, and FED/AMS-coded records side by side so we can judge which setup actually captures clinically plausible missed opportunities before I defend this internally.
turns.utterance: I think the fastest way through this is a focused audit set. Let's pull a small sample of cases with next-day admission, observation-home discharge, and FED or AMS coding, then compare how they behave under the different linkage choices. That should tell us which implementation best matches the intended antecedent visit concept.

turns.inner_thought: That's reasonable. I'll produce side-by-side reruns so we can isolate the source of the discrepancy without hand-tuning the whole pipeline: alternate hospitalization anchors, strict versus broader treat-and-release logic, and current script versus expanded FED/AMS mapping. Then we'll have defensible audit tables for the review group.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll set up side-by-side reruns before the methods review: alternate hospitalization anchors, observation-inclusive versus stricter treat-and-release logic, and the current versus expanded FED/AMS mapping. I'll also generate audit tables so we can see exactly which cases move under each version.
